title: Luck vs skill
summary: Why the best of many backtests is usually luck, how the deflated Sharpe ratio and placebo tests catch it, and the 11 tests every Parity strategy runs through, shown on the carry strategy's real numbers.

lessons.title: Random paths
body: Imagine 39 strategies that know nothing. Each day each one gains or loses at random, as bumpy as Parity's currency **carry** strategy, 3.9% a year, but with no real gain. None has any skill.

Run them over the same 27 years as carry's real record, 2000 to 2026, and they fan out. The best turns $100 into $148. Carry's real result is $149. On a chart, that much luck and a real effect look the same.
Time does not fix this quickly. For a Sharpe ratio of 0.5, telling it apart from zero takes roughly 16 years of data. Carry's Sharpe ratio is 0.39, so even 27 years leaves it only just clear of zero.

visual.alt: Real and simulated. 39 simulated strategies with no skill, each as bumpy as carry, fan out from $100 between 2000 and 2026. The best ends at $148 and the worst at $65. Carry's real record, drawn on top, ends at $149.

steps.caption: One simulated strategy with no skill, as bumpy as carry. Its path wanders by chance.
steps.title: One strategy with no skill

steps.caption: Ten of them. Some end up, some down.
steps.title: Ten with no skill

steps.caption: 39 of them, one for each idea Parity counted in its first official run. The best ends at $148.
steps.title: 39 with no skill

steps.caption: Carry's real record over the same years: $100 became $149.
Carry ends $1 above the best no-skill path.
steps.verdict: Carry ends at $149. The best of 39 no-skill paths ends at $148. On a chart, luck and skill look the same.

inParity.label: Strategy search: every variation tried, best first

check.q: 39 strategies with no skill are run for 27 years. What do you expect?
options: Some end well up by luck alone
check.why: Random paths spread out. In the picture the best of 39 turns $100 into $148 with no skill at all.

check.q: Roughly how many years does it take to tell a Sharpe of 0.5 apart from zero?
check.why: The t-statistic is about the Sharpe ratio times the square root of the years. 0.5 times the square root of 16 is 2.

check.q: Carry ends at $149 and the best no-skill path at $148. What does the chart alone tell you?
options: Not enough to tell skill from luck
check.why: A result this close to the best lucky path cannot separate the two. The tests in the next lessons can.

lessons.title: The best of many tries
body: Trying many variations of an idea and keeping the best is called **multiple testing**, or data snooping. Every changed setting counts as a try, even the ones you forgot about.
The picture shows the Sharpe ratios of 1,000 strategies with zero real skill, each over 10 years. Most land near zero. The best of the 1,000 scores 0.96, which would look excellent on its own.
So the question is never only "how good is this backtest?". It is "how good is it compared with the best I would expect from that many tries with no skill?".

visual.alt: A histogram of the Sharpe ratios of 1,000 strategies with no skill, each over 10 years, centred on zero. 95% of them land between -0.60 and 0.63. The best of the 1,000, marked, scores 0.96.

params.beatLabel: Of the no-skill tries it beats

steps.caption: 1,000 strategies with no skill, 10 years each. Each bar counts how many scored that Sharpe ratio.
95% of them land between -0.60 and 0.63. That spread is luck alone.
Keep only the best: the best of 10 scores 0.58, the best of 100 0.69 and the best of all 1,000 0.96.
More tries give luck more chances, so the best one keeps climbing.
steps.verdict: The best of 1,000 no-skill tries scores 0.96. That is the score a backtest has to beat.

inParity.label: Edge Lab: the lesson on multiple testing

check.q: Why does trying more variations make the best backtest look better?
options: More tries give luck more chances to produce a high score
check.why: The maximum of many random results grows with the number of tries.

check.q: Which of these counts as a separate try?
options: Every setting you changed and tested
check.why: Each tested variation is a chance for luck. Counting only the final one makes it look rarer than it is.

lessons.title: The deflated Sharpe ratio
body: The **deflated Sharpe ratio** raises the bar for every extra try. It gives the chance, from 0 to 1, that a strategy's true Sharpe is above the best you would expect from that many unskilled tries. It also allows for fat tails and a short history.
Parity wants at least 0.95 before a strategy counts as beating the market on that test. A strategy that would pass if it were the only idea tried can fail once the other tries are counted.

Carry is a real example. Its Sharpe ratio over 27 years is 0.39, which clears the bar for a single try, 0.31. But Parity counted 39 tries, and the best of 39 unskilled tries averages 0.41. Carry's deflated Sharpe is 0.44, well short of 0.95. The formula is from Bailey and Lopez de Prado (2014).

visual.alt: Real and simulated. A histogram of the Sharpe ratios of 1,000 simulated strategies with no skill over 27 years. A dashed line at 0.31 marks the bar for a single try. Carry's real Sharpe ratio, 0.39, clears it. A shaded range from 0.28 to 0.57 shows where the best of 39 no-skill tries lands nine times in ten, and carry sits inside it.

params.beatLabel: Of the no-skill tries it beats

steps.caption: 1,000 simulated strategies with no skill, each over the same 27 years as carry. Each bar counts how many scored that Sharpe ratio.
Carry's real Sharpe ratio is 0.39. Against a single try it clears the bar of 0.31.
But Parity counted 39 tries. Nine times in ten, the best of 39 no-skill tries lands between 0.28 and 0.57.
Carry sits inside that range, just under its average of 0.41.
steps.verdict: Carry's deflated Sharpe is 0.44, short of the 0.95 bar. Counting all 39 tries, its 0.39 may be luck.

inParity.label: The 11 tests, including the deflated Sharpe

check.q: What does a deflated Sharpe ratio of 0.95 mean?
options: About a 95% chance the true Sharpe beats the best expected from that many unskilled tries
check.why: It is a probability, adjusted for the number of tries, fat tails and the length of the history.

check.q: You tested 39 variations. Compared with testing one, the bar to pass is:
check.why: More tries mean luck reaches higher, so the bar rises.

check.q: Carry's Sharpe ratio is 0.39 and the best of 39 lucky tries averages 0.41. Why does carry fail this test?
options: Its Sharpe ratio is below zero
Luck alone, over 39 tries, usually scores about as high
check.why: With 39 tries counted, 0.39 is about what the luckiest no-skill try reaches, so its deflated Sharpe is only 0.44.

lessons.title: The placebo test
body: A **placebo test** runs a copy of the strategy that cannot know anything. Parity keeps the strategy's positions, size and trading, but slides them to random dates at least a year away. Timing is destroyed; everything else stays the same.

It does this 500 times. If the real strategy's timing matters, it should beat at least 95% of those copies. If it only does as well as the random-date copies, its result came from something other than timing, such as just being in the market.

The test is hard on slow strategies. Carry holds similar positions for years, so a copy shifted by a year often still holds the right currencies. In Parity's first official run, 32 of carry's 500 copies did at least as well as the real thing, so it failed by a small margin.

visual.alt: Real results from Parity's first official run. A histogram of the Sharpe ratios of 500 copies of the carry strategy moved to random dates, centred on 0.25. 95% of copies score below 0.41. Carry on its real dates, marked, scores 0.39. 32 copies, 6%, score at least as well.

steps.caption: Carry's real positions, slid to 500 random dates. Each bar counts copies with that Sharpe ratio.
95% of the copies score below 0.41. That is the bar.
Carry on its real dates scores 0.39, just under the bar.
32 of the 500 copies score at least as well.
steps.verdict: 6% of random-date copies match carry's real timing. The bar is under 5%, so carry fails the placebo test.

check.q: What does Parity's placebo test change?
options: Only the dates of the positions
check.why: Positions, size and trading stay the same. Only the timing is moved to random dates.

check.q: To pass, the real strategy must beat what share of the 500 random-date copies?
check.why: The bar is 95%, the usual level for a p-value of 0.05.

check.q: 6% of the random-date copies do at least as well as carry. Does it pass?
options: Yes, it beats most of the copies
No, fewer than 5% may match it
check.why: The bar is that fewer than 5% of the copies match the real result. Carry misses it by a small margin.

lessons.title: The 11 tests
body: Every Parity strategy runs the same 11 tests, set before any results were seen. Six ask whether it beats the S&P 500: better return for the risk, more money at the same risk, the deflated Sharpe, double costs, every era and the last five years.
Five ask whether anything is real at all: a range of results clearly above zero, the placebo, nearby settings, removing the best year, and how it does in the stock market's worst months.

A strategy can fail the first group and pass the second. That means a real effect that is too small to beat stocks on its own, which can still be useful. Carry, in Parity's first official run, passed none of the six A tests and three of the five B tests: 3 of 11.

visual.alt: Real results from Parity's first official run, for the carry strategy. Beats the S&P 500: 0 of 6 tests. Anything real: 3 of 5 tests. Sharpe ratio 95% range: 0.00 to 0.75. Deflated Sharpe: 0.44 against a bar of 0.95. 3 of 11 tests passed.

stats.label: Anything real
stats.note: Above zero, nearby settings, without its best year

stats.label: Sharpe ratio, 95% range
stats.note: From 1,000 reshuffled versions of its history

steps.caption: Carry in Parity's first official run. Group A asks whether it beats the S&P 500. It passes none of six.
Group B asks whether anything is real. It passes three of five: above zero, nearby settings and without its best year.
Replayed on 1,000 reshuffled histories, its Sharpe ratio stays between 0.00 and 0.75. Counting 39 tries, the deflated Sharpe is 0.44.
3 of 11 tests passed.
steps.verdict: Some signs of a real effect, not enough to rely on. Carry does not beat the S&P 500.

inParity.label: Official record: only pre-registered runs count

check.q: Carry fails all six A tests and passes three of the five B tests. What is its verdict?
options: Some signs of a real effect, not enough to rely on
check.why: Group B finds some signs of a real effect, but two B tests fail and no A test passes.

check.q: When were the pass marks for the 11 tests set?
check.why: Fixing the bar first means it cannot be bent to fit a result. Changing one needs a decision written first.
If the result disappears without its best year, it may come from one event.
